title: Winding a centre-pull ball
subtitle: By hand, with a nostepinne, and with a ball winder
excerpt: Yarn from a skein needs to be wound before you can use it without tangles. A centre-pull ball lets you draw yarn from the inside, so the ball sits still as you work rather than rolling across the floor. Three methods give the same result with different tools.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A length of yarn wound into a loose, open loop and twisted on itself for sale. Must be wound into a ball before use, otherwise it tangles as you pull from it.
A ball of yarn with the working end buried in the centre, so you can draw yarn from the inside without the ball rolling.
An expandable frame that holds a skein open under tension while you wind from it. Prevents the skein collapsing into tangles.

content.text: A
centre-pull ball

is a wound ball of yarn that feeds from the middle rather than from the outside. When you pull the working end from the centre, the ball sits still; a ball that feeds from the outside rolls around and gathers dust. Any
skein
needs to be wound before use, and the centre-pull method is the most practical way to do it.
What you need

items.name: Your thumb and fingers (hand-winding method)
items.note: No extra tools needed. Slow but reliable for small quantities.

items.name: Nostepinne
items.note: A wooden peg or dowel roughly 25 cm long and 2.5 cm in diameter. Traditional Scandinavian yarn tool. Produces a consistent centre-pull ball.

items.name: Ball winder and swift
items.note: A ball winder is a hand-cranked device that winds a ball quickly and evenly. Pair it with a swift to hold the skein open while winding. The fastest method for large skeins.

items.name: Chair back
items.note: A stand-in for a swift if you do not have one. Drape the skein over the chair back and wind from it.

content.text: Method 1: by hand
Hold the yarn end between your thumb and forefinger, leaving a 15 cm tail. This tail becomes the centre-pull end.
Wrap the yarn around your thumb and two fingers held together, making a figure of eight. Do this about 20 times to build a small core bundle.
Fold the bundle in half and slip it off your fingers, keeping the tail end free at the centre.
Continue winding the remaining yarn around the outside of this core, turning the bundle in your hand as you go to build an even ball. Do not wind too tightly; the yarn should be relaxed on the ball.
Tuck the last few centimetres under a nearby wrap to secure. The tail at the centre is the working end.
Method 2: with a nostepinne
Tie the yarn end around the nostepinne near the top, leaving a tail of 20 cm hanging free at the end of the nostepinne. This becomes the centre pull.

Wind the yarn diagonally around the nostepinne at a 45-degree angle, working from the top towards the bottom. After 10 to 15 wraps, reverse the angle and wind back upwards. Continue reversing direction every 10 to 15 wraps.
Turn the nostepinne in your non-dominant hand as you wind, spreading the yarn evenly.
When all the yarn is wound, slide the ball off the nostepinne. The nostepinne leaves a cavity in the centre; the tail threaded through this cavity is the working end.
Method 3: with a ball winder and swift
Set up the
swift

and drape the open skein over it. Expand the swift to hold the skein under gentle tension. Thread the end of the yarn through the ball winder's yarn guide and attach it to the winder's central peg. Crank the ball winder handle at a steady pace; the swift rotates to feed the yarn. The winder produces a uniform cake-shaped centre-pull ball. Remove the cake from the peg by sliding it off; the centre pull is the end that was attached to the peg.
Common problems

items.symptom: The ball collapses inward as you pull from the centre
items.cause: The centre core is too small or was wound too loosely, so the ball has no structure to hold itself up once the yarn is used up.
items.fix: Build a larger core at the start , about 20 to 30 hand-winds before folding and beginning the outer wrap. On ball-winder cakes this is less common because the cone shape provides support.

items.symptom: The yarn is stretching and losing elasticity on the ball
items.cause: The yarn was wound under tension, which stretches the fibres and causes the yarn to spring back when released during crocheting.
items.fix: Wind more loosely. The yarn should sit on the ball without being pulled taut. When in doubt, let the ball rotate in your hand as you wind rather than holding it still.

items.cause: The skein was not held open while winding, causing loops to cross over each other.
items.fix: Stop and untangle before continuing. On future skeins, use a swift or chair back to hold the skein open under gentle tension throughout the winding process.

content.text: What to try next

Once the ball is wound, check it by pulling from the centre: the yarn should feed smoothly without resistance. If the ball collapses or tangles on the first pull, the centre core was too small. Wind a new one with a larger core before starting the project.
